findings.title: Backup code single-use enforcement is not atomic (read-modify-write race)
findings.body: In the credentials authorize() handler, the backup-code check does a read of the decrypted backupCodes array, an indexOf lookup, and then a separate prisma.user.update that writes back the whole array. Two concurrent sign-in requests using the same backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so one single-use code authenticates twice; likewise two concurrent logins with different codes will each write their own copy of the array and the last write wins, resurrecting a code the other request already consumed. The code is also consumed (nulled and persisted) before next-auth finishes creating the session, so any later failure (JWT encode error, network drop mid-request) burns the code without a successful login. Single-use consumption should be made atomic/transactional and only committed once authentication has succeeded.

findings.title: onEnable is only invoked via the "Close" button; dismissing the dialog any other way leaves the 2FA switch out of sync
findings.body: After a successful enable, the modal moves to the DisplayBackupCodes step and onEnable() (which updates the settings page state, e.g. the two-factor switch) is only called from the "Close" button's onClick. If the user closes the dialog via ESC, the dialog's built-in close affordance, or onOpenChange (all wired directly to the onOpenChange prop), neither onEnable nor onCancel fires and the modal state is not reset. The security settings page will continue to show 2FA as disabled even though it is actually enabled in the database, and the dialog's internal step state persists for the next open. Previously onEnable was called directly on the successful enable response, so this is a regression introduced by deferring it to a user click.

findings.title: Existing 2FA users can never obtain backup codes, and the error message tells them to do the impossible
findings.body: Backup codes are only generated in the setup endpoint, which returns 400 TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled for any user who already has 2FA enabled. Users who enabled 2FA before this deploy have backupCodes = null, so the "Lost access" login path and the backup-code disable path always fail for them with MissingBackupCodes. The accompanying message ("No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." in common.json) is misleading because there is no settings flow that generates codes while 2FA is enabled — the only path is to disable 2FA (using the TOTP they may have lost) and re-enable it. Either a regeneration endpoint is needed or the message must tell the user their actual recovery option.

findings.title: No tests for the core new functionality: logging in and disabling 2FA with a backup code
findings.body: The e2e changes only exercise the backup-codes display step (download filename, copy toast, close button). None of the actually risky new code paths are tested: signing in with a backup code, a backup code being consumed (single-use), the incorrect-backup-code error path, the missing-backup-codes error path, or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The file itself contains a TODO acknowledging this, and the PR checklist states no tests were added for the feature. These server-side flows (including the code-consumption logic in next-auth-options.ts) can regress silently.

findings.title: tabIndex={-1} on the password visibility toggle removes keyboard access
findings.body: The show/hide password toggle button in PasswordField now has tabIndex={-1}, making it unreachable by keyboard in every password field across the app (login, 2FA setup/disable, etc.). Keyboard-only users can no longer verify what they typed into a password field. If the goal was to stop Enter on the toggle from submitting the surrounding form, the button already has type="button"; excluding it from tab order is an accessibility regression rather than a fix.
